week.t: Science News Explores: four footprints in North Dakota are the first adult T. rex trackway; walking pace about 1.6 m/s
NASA: Chandra finds a hidden black hole or neutron star feeding the 113-day outbursts of the star AT 2016blu
NASA: the station crew packs a Dragon cargo craft with mould samples and a spacesuit for return next week
Physics World: a 3° limit on how well δ-CP, the neutrino–antineutrino angle, can ever be measured
Quanta: QT45, a 45-nucleotide RNA that copies other RNA strands, found in a pool of 10 trillion
India’s DST: the star cluster UBC 63, 4,892 light-years away, is really two clusters that passed within 23 light-years

tiles.cap: A star 30 million light-years away flares every 113 days. X-rays found what was robbing it
tiles.nums: between the outbursts of the star AT 2016blu; at least 27 of them were recorded between 2012 and 2026
tiles.p1: For 15 years astronomers watched a star in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years away, brighten like a supernova and then survive, over and over. The star, AT 2016blu, is a luminous blue variable, a type sometimes called a “supernova impostor”, with at least 33 times the Sun’s mass. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has now found the cause: a previously hidden companion, either a black hole or a neutron star, that pulls material off the star every 113 days as the two orbit each other.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA published the result on Monday 9 November; the paper is in The Astrophysical Journal.
deep: Caught at the right time

Chandra observed the star on 24 to 27 March 2026, after optical telescopes saw an outburst begin, under its “Target of Opportunity” programme. In X-rays the star was at least 100 times brighter than in 2001 to 2002, before the outbursts started. Lead author Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia: “Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen.”
Why Chandra

A nearby bright X-ray source sits close to AT 2016blu on the sky, and NASA says Chandra is the only X-ray telescope with vision sharp enough to tell the two apart. The page calls this the first X-ray detection of this class of erupting star, and the first found with a black hole or neutron star companion.
Amateurs counted the bursts

The optical record came from the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope, the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Supernova Project and the American Association of Variable Star Observers, including data from more than 30 amateur astronomers. Co-author Núria Torres-Albà: “This star’s behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly it’s not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year.”
The picture
The image combines Chandra X-rays with a Sloan Digital Sky Survey optical view of NGC 4559. The best-known luminous blue variable is Eta Carinae, in our own galaxy.
tiles.src: NASA / Chandra X-ray Center, 9 Nov 2026 (Megan Watzke): NASA’s Chandra Finds Source of Star’s Mysterious Outbursts · The Astrophysical Journal (Aghakhanloo et al.)
tiles.credit: Image: X-ray NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al.; optical SDSS; processing NASA/CXC/SAO/P. Edmonds

tiles.cap: A spacesuit, station mould, drinking water: what the crew is packing into Dragon
tiles.nums: in space, across two expeditions, for NASA’s Jessica Watkins on 31 October; the photo shows her marking it with a tray of sweets
tiles.p1: NASA’s station blog for Monday 9 November says the Expedition 75 crew began the week packing a SpaceX Dragon cargo craft to return to Earth next week. Flight engineer Anil Menon examined colonies of bacteria, mould and fungi grown from samples swabbed off station surfaces, measured and photographed them, and packed them for return. Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney unpacked a newly delivered spacesuit, checked it and readied it for the Quest airlock, then moved another suit into Dragon so engineers on the ground can examine it.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: nearly everything that goes up must be counted, swabbed, photographed and, if it is worth the seat, brought back down.
deep: Water and breath

Canadian Space Agency flight engineer Joshua Kutryk collected samples of the station’s drinking water for microbial analysis on Earth. Roscosmos flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov recorded his breathing rate wearing an acoustic monitor around his neck, for research on how weightlessness affects the respiratory system.
Housekeeping in orbit

Station commander Pyotr Dubrov photographed mountains, volcanoes and deserts in South America and Africa. Anna Kikina checked docking mechanisms, cleaned smoke detectors and serviced life-support gear.
What NASA did not say

The blog gives no undocking or splashdown date and no mission number for this Dragon, only “next week”. The crew of seven: Dubrov, Kikina and Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos, Menon, Watkins and Delaney of NASA, and Kutryk of the CSA.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 9 Nov 2026: Crew Packing Dragon for Return with Experiments and a Spacesuit

tiles.cap: A star cluster 4,892 light-years away turned out to be two, fresh from a near miss
tiles.nums: the closest approach of the two clusters, about 6 million years ago; today they are about 85 light-years apart and drifting away from each other
tiles.p1: UBC 63 is a sparse open cluster in our galaxy, about 4,892 light-years from Earth, and it was catalogued as one object. A team led by Indian astronomers has found it is two: UBC 63A, about 21 million years old, and UBC 63B, about 562 million years old. The clue was a chance finding in the cluster’s colour-magnitude diagram, the chart of star colour against brightness, which showed two distinct sequences where one cluster would show one.
tiles.p2: Why now: announced by India’s Department of Science and Technology on 5 November; the paper is in The Astronomical Journal.
deep: Rewinding the flyby

Using ESA’s Gaia measurements, machine learning and dynamical simulations run on high-performance computers, the team traced the two clusters back. When the younger one formed they were about 60 parsecs apart (about 196 light-years); about 6 million years ago they passed within about 7 parsecs (about 23 light-years); today they are about 26 parsecs apart (about 85 light-years).
Not a pair for keeps

The two clusters are not gravitationally bound, so they are drifting apart. Lead author Samrat Biswas is an INSPIRE Senior Research Fellow at Gauhati University; co-authors include Biman J. Medhi (Gauhati), Sukanta Deb (Cotton University), H. S. Das (Assam University) and Maheswar Gopinathan and Ram Sagar of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, with collaborators in Italy, China and Japan.
Read it yourself

A colour-magnitude diagram puts each star’s colour across and its brightness up. Stars born together trace one curve; two curves mean two birthdays. That is the whole trick, and it works on a chart you can draw by hand.
tiles.src: PIB / Department of Science and Technology, 5 Nov 2026: Team led by Indian astronomers redefine star cluster UBC 63 as a double cluster system spotted after close flyby · The Astronomical Journal, doi 10.3847/1538-3881/ae8c38

tiles.cap: Flash, then count. Every 5 seconds before the thunder is a mile of air. Test it today
tiles.nums: NOAA’s rule: count the seconds from flash to thunder and divide by 5 for miles; 1 mile is 1.6 km, so about 3 seconds for each kilometre
tiles.p1: Light reaches you from a lightning flash almost instantly; the sound takes about 5 seconds for every mile, says the US National Weather Service, so 15 seconds means the strike was about 3 miles off, and no gap at all means very close. NOAA says thunder is usually heard only out to about 10 miles, and lightning can strike that far from a storm, which is why its rule is simple: if you hear thunder, lightning is close enough to strike you. Count from indoors.
tiles.p2: Why here: Singapore is in its inter-monsoon weeks, which NEA said would bring moderate to heavy thundery showers over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days of early November.
deep: Why sound is slow

Feynman’s lecture on sound shows that the speed of sound in a gas depends only on its temperature, not on the pressure or density, and that it runs at roughly 1/√3 of the average speed of the gas molecules themselves: sound is carried by the motion of the molecules, so it travels at about their own pace.
Newton got it wrong

Newton assumed the air in a sound wave stays at one temperature as it is squeezed. Feynman calls the result the isothermal speed of sound, and wrong. Laplace fixed it: the squeeze is so quick that heat has no time to flow, so each compression also warms, and the wave moves faster than Newton predicted.
The 30/30 rule

Weather Service offices say to head indoors when you cannot count to 30 between flash and thunder, and to stay there 30 minutes after the last clap. A sharp crack means the channel passed nearby; a long rumble means it was at least several miles away.
How hot

The air in a lightning channel may reach 50,000 °F, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, says NOAA. That sudden heating is what makes the air expand with a bang. The US sees about 25 million lightning flashes a year.
tiles.src: NOAA / National Weather Service lightning safety pages (Thunder; Understanding Lightning Science; NWS Shreveport and Melbourne 30/30 rule) · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 47 · NEA advisory, 29 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: A hundred trillion neutrinos crossed you while you read this. Physicists want one angle
tiles.nums: the best precision quantum theory allows on the angle δ-CP from about 1,000 neutrino and antineutrino events; the DUNE experiment, due in 2028, is projected to reach 7–18°
tiles.p1: The Sun alone sends about a hundred trillion neutrinos through your body every second, says CERN, and a typical one could cross a light-year of solid lead without hitting anything. Catching a few is how physicists hope to measure δ-CP, an angle between 0° and 360° that says whether neutrinos and antineutrinos behave differently: 0° or 180° means no difference, 90° or 270° means the biggest possible one. Michela Ignoti, a PhD student at the University of Milan: “A CP-violating phase is connected to the matter-antimatter imbalance in the universe.”
tiles.p2: Why now: Physics World reported on Monday 9 November that Ignoti and Claudia Frugiuele have worked out the ultimate limit on how well that angle can ever be measured.
deep: The ceiling

Using quantum-information theory, the Milan pair find that about 1,000 neutrino and antineutrino events could, in principle, fix δ-CP to about 3°. That is a theoretical ceiling, not a measurement; their paper has been accepted by Physical Review Letters.
Where the information hides

Beam experiments such as T2K in Japan, and the coming Hyper-Kamiokande, look mostly at the first oscillation peak, where neutrinos are most likely to have changed type. The extra information sits at the second maximum, where there are far fewer events. Patrick Huber of Virginia Tech, who was not involved: “the event rates in the second oscillation maximum are much, much smaller … About 10 times smaller at least.”
Who is listening

DUNE, in the United States, is projected to pin δ-CP to within 7–18° after it comes online in 2028, depending on the true value. JUNO in China began its first data run last year and can read the first and tenth oscillation peaks. Huber thinks the new result is unlikely to send experiment designers back to the drawing board.
Feel the number
Count one second. About a hundred trillion solar neutrinos went through you, and almost certainly none of them touched a single atom. The photo shows a prototype of DUNE’s liquid-argon detector.
tiles.src: Physics World, 9 Nov 2026 (Jacklin Kwan): Quantum information reveals limits of neutrino flavour measurements · CERN, 20 Jul 2026 (Davide De Biasio): The puzzle of neutrinos, seventy years on
tiles.credit: Photo: Marina Cavazza / CERN, via Physics World

tiles.cap: Earbuds that record what you just heard. Maker says 10 hours; the tester got 4.5 with ANC
tiles.nums: of flash memory inside Nothing’s Ear (3a) earbuds, enough to hold audio snapshots of up to a minute and call recordings
tiles.p1: Nothing’s Ear (3a) are $99 earbuds on TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list for one trick: pinch both buds and they save an “audio snapshot” of up to a minute, including up to 30 seconds of what played before you pinched, which the app can replay, transcribe or share. Inside: a 12 mm dynamic driver in each bud, Bluetooth 6.0, three directional microphones per bud, 32 MB of flash storage and an IP54 rating against dust and splashes. TechRadar’s Becky Scarrott lists one bud at 4.53 g and gave the pair 4 out of 5.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the hardware is ordinary; the argument is about what a microphone in your ear should be allowed to remember.
deep: Battery: two stories

Nothing’s launch post says up to 10 hours per charge with noise cancelling off, 6 hours with it on, and 42 hours in total with the case. TechRadar’s spec sheet gives 6 hours with ANC off, 4.5 hours with it on and 25 hours with the case; in testing the reviewer found the 4.5-hour figure “bang on”, and wrote: “In my briefing, I was told the buds themselves would last 10 hours — but that turned out not to be the case.” Battery scored 2.5 of 5.
The privacy problem

The buds can also record a phone call. Nothing says “a privacy notification alerts others when recording during a call or meeting”; TechRadar found “the only indication here that you’re being recorded may be a brief beep” and called covert recording of private conversations “a serious issue”. Its do-not-buy list: “The idea of covert surveillance bothers you.”
What worked

Noise cancelling cuts sound in the human-voice range by up to 6 dB, with peak reduction of 45 dB, says Nothing; TechRadar called the ANC “no slouch” and the sound “fun, upfront”, with LDAC support at $99 “good stuff”. Faults: no wireless charging, “a little bass-heavy at times”, and buds “a little big” for small ears.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Daniel Varghese) · Nothing launch post, Ear (3a) available now, 7 Jul 2026 · TechRadar, 25 Jul 2026 (Becky Scarrott), 4/5

tiles.cap: Four footprints, 66.5 million years old: a T. rex walking at 1.6 metres a second. Match it
tiles.nums: the walking speed worked out from the spacing of the prints, about a brisk human walking pace; each print is about 80 cm across
tiles.p1: Four fossil footprints on a steep slope in North Dakota form the first known trackway, three or more prints in a row, likely made by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex. Their spacing suggests the animal was moving at about 1.6 metres (5.2 feet) per second, which Science News Explores calls a brisk human walking pace. Kent Hups, who teaches at Northglenn High School near Denver and works at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, found the first print while fossil hunting in 2025: three toes, about 80 centimetres across.
tiles.p2: Try it: 1.6 metres a second is 16 metres in 10 seconds. Pace it out along a corridor and see whether you have to hurry.
deep: Only one suspect

The prints are in the Hell Creek Formation and are roughly 66.5 million years old. Adult T. rex reached about 12 metres long. Peter Falkingham of Liverpool John Moores University in England, who led the analysis: “As far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track-maker that could have made these.”
Why it is a first

Before this, only single adult T. rex prints were known, plus trackways from possible juveniles or a related species. The team’s paper appeared in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology on 8 September 2026.
Hedges

The prints are poorly preserved, so the speed estimate could be somewhat too high or too low. A fifth print may still be hidden in the hillside; the team is waiting for erosion to uncover it. Hups: “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 10 Nov 2026 (Erin Garcia de Jesús): Four T. rex footprints hint at how fast it traveled · Falkingham et al., Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, 8 Sep 2026

tiles.cap: A 45-letter molecule that copies other molecules: a hint of how life could have begun
tiles.nums: random RNA molecules in the starting pool from which QT45 and two similar copiers emerged, about a hundred-billionth of all possible sequences of that length
tiles.p1: Modern cells have a chicken-and-egg problem: DNA holds the instructions, proteins do the work, and each needs the other. The “RNA world” idea says RNA once did both jobs. In the late 1980s researchers found RNAs that act as catalysts, named ribozymes, and in 1996 a ribozyme was made that joins RNA building blocks together. Quanta reports that Philipp Holliger’s team at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in the UK has now found QT45 (“quite tiny”), an RNA just 45 nucleotides long that can copy another RNA strand. Holliger: “In principle it can copy any sequence.”
tiles.p2: Why it matters: earlier lab-made copiers were several hundred nucleotides long, while RNAs that assemble on their own have been only about 10 to 15. Forty-five is within reach of chance; Holliger says that “does not seem an unreasonable ask”.
deep: Why size matters

Gerald Joyce’s group at the Salk Institute evolved ribozymes in the lab in 2019, but mutations tended to destroy their catalytic activity, which suggested self-sustaining RNA evolution is hard. Holliger started with RNAs of 20 to 40 nucleotides and searched a pool of about 10 trillion random molecules; QT45 and two other small copiers turned up.
Ice and acid
Holliger’s team has shown that cycles of changing acidity plus freezing and thawing can drive RNA replication exponentially, conditions that may have existed near the icy poles of the young Earth.
The catches

Quanta’s caveats: an RNA world might not count as alive, since life also needs a metabolism, and nobody knows whether a suitable niche existed on the early Earth. Copying errors, though, would give RNA what Darwinian evolution needs: variation to select from.
tiles.src: Quanta Magazine, 9 Nov 2026 (Philip Ball): Did Life Begin in an RNA World?

tiles.cap: Two coins, one eye. Slide them until they look the same size, then open the other eye
tiles.p1: Take two coins of different sizes, a 50-cent and a 5-cent coin will do. Close one eye, hold one coin in each hand against a bright, plain background, and move them towards or away from you until they look exactly the same size. Now open both eyes: the trick collapses, and you see a small coin close and a big coin far. The Exploratorium’s point: with one eye closed, your depth perception is almost nonexistent, so your brain cannot tell a small near thing from a big far one.
tiles.p2: Why it works: if two objects look the same size and you know one is farther away, your brain decides the far one is larger. Take away the distance clue and it has nothing to decide with.
deep: Silhouettes help

The Exploratorium says a very bright, solid-coloured background works best, so the coins appear in silhouette and their features cannot be made out. Detail on the coin faces is a size clue; remove it and the illusion gets stronger.
Two eyes, two viewpoints
With both eyes open you gather more information and more points of view, so you judge size, shape and distance more accurately. One eye gives you a flat picture; two give you the geometry.
Where nature uses it

The pupa of the butterfly Spalgis epius carries a pattern like a rhesus macaque’s face and is only about half as wide as a fingernail, yet it seems to scare off birds, which may read it as a bigger, more distant monkey. And the Sun is far larger than the Moon but far farther away: their apparent sizes are nearly equal, which is why the Moon can almost exactly cover the Sun in a total eclipse.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Size and Distance

tiles.cap: Both Mars probes fired on time: two 9-minute burns, two days apart, and they are gone
tiles.nums: powered Earth flybys: 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 Nov about 1,000 miles up, and 6 am on Monday 9 Nov about 650 miles up
tiles.p1: NASA says both twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have completed their powered Earth flybys and are on their way to Mars. The first fired its roughly 9-minute trans-Mars injection burn at 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, when it was about 1,000 miles above Earth’s surface; the second did the same at 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November (7 pm in Singapore), about 650 miles up. Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for the Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters: “This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we’ve now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days.”
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Jeff Parker of Advanced Space, the lead mission designer, says the loiter-and-flyby route “provides the flexibility to launch almost anytime and then use Earth’s gravity to get a boost to Mars” instead of waiting every two years for the planets to line up.
deep: The route

ESCAPADE launched on 13 November 2025 from Cape Canaveral, when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun. The pair spent about a year in a loiter orbit around Lagrange point 2, about a million miles from Earth, then swung back past Earth so that its gravity plus the engine burn could throw them towards Mars.
Ten months to go

The cruise to Mars takes about 10 months, with trajectory correction manoeuvres along the way. Orbit insertion burns are planned for 7 and 9 September 2027, each spacecraft firing its engine for about 11 minutes, and science operations are expected to begin in June 2028.
Two orbiters, one planet

Rob Lillis of the University of California, Berkeley, the principal investigator: “This will be the first science mission to choreograph two orbiters around Mars.” The goal is to measure how the solar wind, a million-mile-per-hour stream of material from the Sun, drives the loss of the Martian atmosphere, from two places at once.
What is aboard

Each orbiter weighs about 209 kg dry and 535 kg fuelled, and carries an electrostatic analyser from UC Berkeley, a magnetometer from NASA Goddard, a Langmuir probe from Embry-Riddle and student-built cameras from Northern Arizona University. They rode to space on the second flight of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket.
tiles.src: NASA, 9 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas): NASA’s ESCAPADE Completes Powered Earth Flybys, Now En Route to Mars · NASA ESCAPADE mission page
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger, via NASA

tiles.cap: NASA is hiring astronauts. Last time, more than 8,000 people applied and 10 got in
tiles.nums: applicants were chosen for NASA’s 2025 astronaut class; applications for the next class opened on Saturday
tiles.p1: NASA opened applications on Saturday 7 November for its next class of astronauts, who it says will join the agency as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. US citizens have until 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December to submit their applications, and NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027. The agency last opened applications in 2024: from more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are now completing nearly two years of training.
tiles.p2: Why now: applications opened on Saturday 7 November and close at 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December; final selection is expected in late 2027, when training begins.
deep: The numbers
Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates. The agency has 32 astronauts active in its astronaut corps today.
If you want to fly it

For pilots, NASA lists 750 hours as pilot in command of high-performance jet aircraft, or 1,500 total flight hours in other fixed-wing aircraft including 750 as pilot in command, or 1,000 total flight hours in rotary-wing aircraft including 300 as pilot in command. Only US citizens can apply.
What they said

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, adding that the missions “will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage.” Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson put it shorter: “The window is open. The mission is waiting.”
Who picks

Scott Tingle, chief astronaut, chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston; for those who apply, he says, becoming a NASA astronaut “is more than a career opportunity”. The photo shows NASA announcing its 2025 astronaut candidate class at Johnson on 22 September 2025.
tiles.src: NASA news release 26-093, 7 Nov 2026 · NASA media advisory M26-084 (MAX POWER key events), updated 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Pena is still the only storm on the hurricane maps: 40 mph, 1,400 km southwest of Honolulu
tiles.nums: maximum sustained winds (65 km/h) of Tropical Storm Pena at 11 am Hawaii time on Tuesday 10 November, its 17th advisory; central pressure 1004 millibars
tiles.p1: On Tuesday the US National Hurricane Center listed no tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and none in the eastern Pacific. The only one on its maps was Tropical Storm Pena in the central Pacific, about 870 miles (1,400 km) southwest of Honolulu and about 500 miles (805 km) southeast of Johnston Island, moving west-southwest at 9 mph with 40 mph winds. Its advisory headline: “PENA TURNING WEST-SOUTHWEST OVER THE CENTRAL PACIFIC”.
tiles.p2: Why now: a quiet week on the hurricane maps in a year in which the northwest Pacific had 25 named storms by late October, according to NASA Earth Observatory.
deep: By the numbers

Pena was at 10.8°N 165.2°W at 11 am Hawaii time on Tuesday. Tropical-storm-force winds extended up to 115 miles (185 km) from the centre; there were no watches or warnings and no land hazards. The forecast: “A turn to the west and then west-northwest is expected over the next couple of days” and “Little change in strength is forecast over the next several days.”
The other ocean

NASA Earth Observatory’s 3 November feature: the northwest Pacific had 25 named storms by late October 2026. Super Typhoon In-fa was an “annular” storm, a type that makes up about 4% of western North Pacific cyclones and whose eyes average about 45 km across against a typical 25 km; Typhoon Champi’s winds reached nearly 300 km/h. NASA Goddard meteorologist Gary Partyka calls the strong El Niño a “likely contributor”.
Reading an advisory
This was public advisory number 17, issued at 11 am Hawaii Standard Time (2100 UTC, 5 am Wednesday in Singapore). The pressure was 1004 mb. Advisories come every six hours while a storm lives.
tiles.src: NOAA National Hurricane Center / Central Pacific Hurricane Center, Tropical Storm Pena Public Advisory 17, 11 am HST Tue 10 Nov 2026; NHC Atlantic and eastern Pacific outlooks, Tue 10 Nov 2026 · NASA Earth Observatory, 3 Nov 2026: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
tiles.credit: Image: NOAA / NHC–CPHC, central Pacific seven-day outlook (live)

tiles.cap: Chatbots raised on American English “correct” Indian English. An NUS dean weighs in
tiles.p1: Much of the language data that AI models learn from is American English, and NUS News reports that users in India have found chatbots “correcting” Indian English expressions as grammatical mistakes. Prof Lionel Wee, Dean of the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences and a sociolinguist, told a panel organised by The Mandala Club on 20 October that meaning depends on context: “Table number five wants their check” or “I’ve got to wash my hair” carry more than their words. He calls himself an “AI agnostic” and urges “a healthy dose of scepticism towards AI”.
tiles.p2: Why here: a Singapore take on the Using AI lane, from a professor who researches how people actually talk.
deep: Who was there

The panel, “Lost in Translation”, was organised by The Mandala Club on 20 October 2026. Alongside Prof Wee were Rahat Kapur, co-founder and editorial director of Beyond The Boardroom, and Chathuni Uduwela, a public policy practitioner.
Comfort from a machine

Two stories from the panel: a colleague’s niece turned to a chatbot for comfort after a breakup, and a student kept using a religious chatbot app long after exams were over. Wee’s question: “Are we creating generations that are less resilient, less able to deal with setbacks and difficulties”.
Like calculators?

NUS News’ comparison: writing reduced the need to memorise, and calculators made manual calculation less necessary. Its question: as AI takes on more thinking tasks, which human skills should we keep cultivating?
Access is not enough
Wee: “Access on its own is not really meaningful if you don’t take into account the kinds of friction that people encounter”.
tiles.src: NUS News, 4 Nov 2026: Is AI changing the way we speak, think and connect with one another?

tiles.cap: A*STAR built a molecule that kills one yeast and spares its close cousins. That is hard
tiles.nums: Candida species killed: C. tropicalis died, while C. albicans, C. auris and C. glabrata were largely spared in mixed cultures
tiles.p1: Broad-spectrum antifungal drugs kill the harmful fungus and can also kill the helpful ones living in you. A*STAR’s Infectious Diseases Labs and Bioinformatics Institute designed Gua-SMACS-16, a synthetic molecule that killed Candida tropicalis while largely sparing mammalian cells, zebrafish embryos and three related yeasts, C. albicans, C. auris and C. glabrata, in mixed cultures. Senior scientist Ning Li: “A narrow-spectrum antifungal could offer important advantages by preserving beneficial fungi in the microbiome”.
tiles.p2: Why now: published in Advanced Science and highlighted by A*STAR Research on Monday.
deep: The tell
The selectivity is linked to β-glucan, a major component of fungal cell walls: C. tropicalis walls contain relatively less β-glucan than the other species tested.
Team-up

Combined with the existing drug caspofungin, Gua-SMACS-16 showed strong synergy against other Candida species, including C. auris, which the WHO designates a critical priority. Yue Wang of A*STAR IDL: “Caspofungin reduces β-glucan production, which may weaken cell walls and allow more Gua-SMACS-16 to reach cell membranes”.
What SMACS means
Synthetic membrane-active cationic supramolecule. Wang: “Gua-SMACS-16 is designed to preferentially bind fungal cells, rather than mammalian ones”.
tiles.src: A*STAR Research, 9 Nov 2026: A targeted SMAC-down on fungal foes · Advanced Science 13 (41), 2026

tiles.cap: A slide-out phone keyboard. The tester typed 30 words a minute on it, 53 on glass
tiles.nums: words per minute on the Clicks keyboard vs the touchscreen in Tom’s Guide’s test; accuracy 62% vs 81%
tiles.p1: Clicks’ Power Keyboard snaps to the magnets on the back of a phone (MagSafe or Qi2) and slides out as a physical keyboard: 119.7 × 76.6 × 15.2 mm, 180 g, with a built-in 2,300 mAh battery that also tops up the phone over 5 W Qi wireless charging. TIME put it on its Best Inventions 2026 list; TIME calls the company “chockablock with BlackBerry alumni”, and says co-founder Jeffrey Gadway obsessively adjusted key curvature, row spacing and actuation points. Tom’s Guide’s Jason England typed 53 words a minute at 81% accuracy on his iPhone’s glass and 30 words a minute at 62% on the Clicks.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: it is a bet that fingers remember what thumbs forgot, and the test says they mostly do not.
deep: Inside

Bluetooth LE 5.4, pairing with up to 9 devices, three of them saved to the 1, 2 and 3 keys. By default 500 mAh of the battery is reserved for the keyboard itself. There is an adjustable LED backlight and a USB-C port, but the battery cannot charge other devices through it.
What went wrong

With the keyboard slid out the phone becomes top-heavy: “I constantly felt like it was going to somersault backward out of my hands.” The reviewer also found a “cheap-feeling plastic back” and a slide-out hinge that “feels almost distressingly loose”, called 2,300 mAh small for a power bank, and 5 W charging slow.
What worked

The keys themselves were “objectively well-made”. As a pocket Bluetooth keyboard it drove a smart TV and a PS5, and it worked with Samsung DeX and Viture glasses. Verdict: “undeniably useful”, “not for everyone”.
Price
The maker’s page says “From $139” with a $30 discount already applied; Tom’s Guide listed it at $99 when the review ran in August.

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at the University of Pennsylvania put it in six words. Do not hand over the things you enjoy and that give you meaning, he says, and decide which skills you want to protect. Trent Cash, a behavioural scientist at the University of Waterloo, adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient, and he does not think AI is going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. Back on their own, they did not detect the growths as well.
The readers who gave up

People who used an AI tool to solve SAT questions were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because persistence is key for learning.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
